anchors.paper_title: Delineating neural contributions to electroencephalogram-based speech decoding
anchors.reason: Title and authors match the dataset exactly; the bioRxiv paper reports the uhd-EEG speech decoding study that produced this data.

metadata.methods_description: 128-channel EEG was recorded with a 10x preamp gain, together with bipolar EOG, EMG of the upper and lower orbicularis oris, microphone, display, and trigger channels (139 channels total). Each trial consisted of 5 repetitions of a single color word at 1.25 s per repetition, in calibration and online decoding sessions.

citation_details.title: Brain-to-Language Decoding: Paradigms, Signals, Methods, Evaluation, Practical Use and Beyond
citation_details.author: Yiqian Yang, Yiqun Duan, Chenyu Liu, Yiqi Wang, Xinliang Zhou, Chin-Teng Lin, Yu Zhang
citation_details.abstract: Brain-to-language decoding translates neural activity associated with language production, internal speech and perception into linguistic or expressive outputs. It offers a route to restoring communication after speech loss and a means of studying how the brain represents language. Advances in neural recording and representation learning have expanded the field from constrained recognition and acoustic reconstruction to text generation, streaming personalised speech and facial animation. This survey synthesises these developments across invasive and non-invasive measurements. We connect Articulated, Inner and Perceived paradigms to the neural populations they engage, the representations available to decoders and the outputs those representations can support. We examine model development, public resources and the evolution of evaluation, and compare published performance and communication costs within their reported protocols. citation_details.title: Delineating neural contributions to electroencephalogram-based speech decoding
citation_details.author: Motoshige Sato, Eri Hatakeyama, Masakazu Inoue, Yasuo Kabe, Sensho Nobe, Akito Yoshida, Atsushi Yamamoto, Yuya Kita, Mayumi Shimizu, Kenichi Tomeoka, Michael X Cohen, Shuntaro Sasai
citation_details.abstract: Abstract Objective . Speech brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as a pivotal technology in facilitating communication for individuals with speech impairments. Utilizing electroencephalography (EEG) for noninvasive speech BCIs offers an accessible and affordable solution, potentially benefiting a broader audience. However, EEG-based speech decoding remains controversial especially for overt speech, due to difficulties in separating speech-related neural activities from myoelectric potential artifacts generated during articulation. Moreover, because paradigms for collecting covert speech data are inherently less scalable than those for overt speech, whether the neural dynamics underlying EEG-based decoding of overt speech are also present during covert speech remains an open and practically important question. Approach . Here we aim to delineate the extent of the neural contributions to EEG-based speech decoding, and the degree to which the underlying neural dynamics are shared across overt and covert speech, by employing Explainable AI techniques to a convolutional neural network predicting spoken words based on signals obtained by ultra-high-density (uhd)-EEG. Main results . We found that electrode-wise contributions to the decoding cannot be explained by their mutual information with electromyography (EMG). Furthermore, contributing periods of speech to EEG-based decoding are distinct from those to decoding solely relying on EMG. Contributing periods of EEG-based decoding partially overlapped between overt and minimally overt speech. Notably, the denoising process successfully enhanced the decoding contribution from electrodes within speech-related brain areas for all speech conditions. Significance . Altogether, our findings support the idea that, with appropriate preprocessing, EEG becomes a valuable tool for decoding spoken words based on underlying neural activities.
